source: Xiong et al. (2025) How Memory Management Impacts LLM Agents: experience-following
finding: Agents with a growing memory copy the outputs of the most similar retrieved record (experience-following). Adding every trajectory (add-all) is worse than a small fixed memory.
numbers: Add-all vs fixed memory: RegAgent success 55.48 vs 67.53; EHRAgent acc 13.05 vs 16.75; AgentDriver 32.32 vs 40.11; CIC-IoT 59.90 vs 71.50. Add-all memory sizes 4100, 2411, 2125, 1050 vs fixed 100, 100, 180, 50. GPT-4o-mini backbone.
quote: high similarity between a task input and the input in a retrieved memory record often results in highly similar agent outputs
limits: Four agents, one backbone for most runs; the synthetic regression agent is not a real task. No formal guarantees.
agent_relevance: Retaining every solved subgoal is worse than keeping few. Retention needs a gate (G3: pass on something the answer was not fitted to).

source: Xiong et al. (2025) selective addition by evaluator quality
finding: Better evaluator gives better retained memory. A strict (human oracle) filter beat every automatic filter. A judge fine-tuned on only 300 trajectories (C3) came close.
limits: Strict judge is a simulated oracle. The vanilla LLM judge C1 was sometimes below the fixed baseline.
agent_relevance: A model-only retention judge is risky; use code-checked outcomes for retain decisions (G5).

source: Xiong et al. (2025) error propagation
finding: Errors in retained records get retrieved, copied and stored again. Against an error-free memory built from ground truth, add-all and coarse-filter runs show a gap that grows over the stream.
numbers: Gap opens at once and widens for add-all and coarse addition. With strict addition AgentDriver started behind, then caught up and passed the error-free variant after about 2000 executions.
limits: Shown on RegAgent and AgentDriver only (Figure 4). AgentDriver ground truth is only relatively correct.
agent_relevance: Wrong retained cases compound. Log which stored record shaped each answer so a bad case can be traced and removed.

source: Xiong et al. (2025) history-based deletion (utility of a case after use)
finding: Delete a case when its average downstream utility over at least n retrievals is low. With a strict evaluator this improved results and cut memory; with a noisy evaluator it was mixed.
numbers: Strict evaluator, no deletion vs history deletion: EHRAgent 38.67 vs 42.06 (mem 1012 vs 784); AgentDriver 51.00 vs 51.81 (1178 vs 846); CIC-IoT 85.40 vs 89.60 (904 vs 788); RegAgent 70.95 vs 69.80. Coarse C1: EHRAgent 25.91 vs 33.55 (1447 vs 1004); CIC-IoT 74.00 vs 73.70.
limits: Needs n retrievals per record before judging (estimation bias). Gains depend on evaluator quality; GPT-4o-mini as the utility judge degraded one agent.
agent_relevance: Modern analogue of Smyth and Keane utility deletion. Case-level outcome tracking beats age-based forgetting.

source: Xiong et al. (2025) periodic and combined deletion; capacity limit
finding: Periodic (age/frequency) deletion cuts memory about 60 to 70 percent with a small loss. Combined deletion keeps most of the gain. With a hard cap equal to the start memory (100 or 180 records), managed memory still beat fixed memory.
numbers: Coarse C1, periodic vs none: EHRAgent mem 1447 to 338 (acc 25.91 to 26.65); AgentDriver 1161 to 426 (36.92 to 36.38); CIC-IoT 1030 to 355 (74.00 to 78.10). Strict combined CIC-IoT mem 904 to 188, acc 85.40 to 85.50.
limits: Cap runs are in appendix figures, not tables. Periodic deletion lost points on RegAgent (63.18 to 60.88).
agent_relevance: Pruning for size is nearly free; pruning for quality needs outcome data. A library of a few hundred cases is enough.

source: Xiong et al. (2025) misaligned experience replay and distribution shift
finding: Some records that passed the filter still mislead (misaligned replay). Deleted records had higher error than retained ones. Under task distribution shift, strict addition and combined deletion stayed near the no-shift level.
numbers: Qualitative KDE of error for deleted vs retained records; gap to the no-shift variant described as small (Figure 7).
limits: Shift built by reordering test sets, not a natural drift.
agent_relevance: A retained case can go stale when the task mix changes; re-score cases after a shift signal (G1).

source: Sarukkai et al. (2025) Self-Generated In-Context Examples (Traj-Bootstrap)
finding: Storing successful agent trajectories and retrieving them raised success a lot, about what 2 to 3 attempts per task give. Returns diminish: most gain comes in the first 25 percent of added tasks.
numbers: Fixed-DB to Traj-Bootstrap (GPT-4o-mini): ALFWorld 0.73 to 0.89; InterCode-SQL 0.75 to 0.79; Wordcraft 0.55 to 0.64. Fixed-DB pass@2 on ALFWorld 0.89.
limits: Success-only storage; failed trajectories left to future work (credit assignment). Within-trial fluctuations show some added trajectories reduce performance.
agent_relevance: Growth has diminishing returns, so a cap is cheap. Store verified wins only.

source: Sarukkai et al. (2025) database-level curation (population-based)
finding: Keep 5 parallel databases; each time size doubles, replace the bottom 20 percent by copies of the top 20 percent. Helps ALFWorld but is noisy early.
numbers: ALFWorld 0.89 to 0.91 (+DB-Curation); with exemplar curation 0.93. Wordcraft 0.64 (no gain). Dips at small database sizes from low-sample quality estimates.
limits: Needs 5 runs; costly. Clear gain on only one of three benchmarks.
agent_relevance: Whole-base selection is expensive and noisy early; prefer cheap per-case utility.

source: Sarukkai et al. (2025) exemplar-level curation: Q(trajectory) = retrieval-weighted outcome
finding: Score each stored trajectory by the average outcome of the tasks where it was retrieved, weighted by retrieval frequency. Keep the best per task. Some trajectories marked successful later cause failures.
numbers: Wordcraft 0.55 to 0.72 (Exemplar-Curation) vs 0.64 plain; InterCode-SQL 0.82 with both vs 0.79 plain; ALFWorld 0.93 combined vs 0.89 plain. Best-per-task databases beat worst-per-task databases at all sizes (Fig 4). GPT-4o-mini alone reaches 0.93 vs AutoManual 0.91 (GPT-4-turbo plus 4o-mini).
limits: Three benchmarks, one backbone; the gain from exemplar curation on ALFWorld alone is small (0.90 vs 0.89).
agent_relevance: Strongest LLM evidence that a Smyth and Keane style per-case utility score works. Keep one best example per problem type, ranked by outcome after retrieval.

source: Suzgun et al. (2025) Dynamic Cheatsheet: uncurated full history vs curated memory
finding: Appending all history (FH) is worse than a self-curated cheatsheet. The curator keeps only useful, generalisable items and can remove wrong or superseded ones.
numbers: AIME 2024: Claude 3.5 Sonnet baseline 23% to DC 50%, while FH gave 26.7%; GPT-4o baseline 20.0% to FH 6.7% to DC-RS 40.0%. Game of 24 GPT-4o 10% to 99% (DC-RS); with empty memory 19%. Claude +9% GPQA-Diamond, +8% MMLU-Pro Eng/Physics.
limits: Curator is the same LLM, with no ground-truth check. GPT-4o-mini and R1/o1 models gain little.
agent_relevance: Curation beats accumulation. Keep memory short and replace entries instead of appending. Needs an outside check on what enters (G3).

source: Suzgun et al. (2025) Dynamic Cheatsheet limits: error clusters and retrieval noise
finding: Errors and corrections cluster in embedding space: one good heuristic helps near neighbours, one bad heuristic poisons them. Loosely related retrieval confuses the model.
numbers: Described qualitatively (Figure 10); GPT-4o dipped on GPQA-Diamond with retrieval.
limits: No numeric test of deletion policies.
agent_relevance: Dedupe by neighbourhood: when a new case lands inside an existing neighbourhood, compare outcomes and keep one.

source: Wei et al. (2026) Evo-Memory benchmark and ReMem
finding: Streaming benchmark of 10 datasets and over 10 memory modules. Simple ExpRAG (retrieve prior experience) is a strong baseline. ReMem adds a Refine step that prunes and reorganises memory.
numbers: Single-turn ReMem: average exact match 0.65, API accuracy 0.85/0.71 (Gemini 2.5 Flash). Multi-turn: BabyAI 0.92/0.96, ScienceWorld 0.95/0.62. Hard-to-easy sequence up to 0.94/0.97 success/progress. Retrieval k=4.
limits: Some table values were garbled in text extraction. Gains in single-turn settings are moderate.
agent_relevance: An explicit refine/prune action in the loop works, but a plain retrieve baseline gets most of the gain. Start simple.

source: Wei et al. (2026) Evo-Memory feedback analysis (RQ4)
finding: When both successes and failures were stored, baselines lost accuracy because naive accumulation added noise and hindered retrieval. ReMem stayed best by refining stored experience.
numbers: Table 3 on AlfWorld and ScienceWorld, Claude and Gemini backbones. Successful experience from harder tasks transfers better (RQ3).
limits: Authors leave failure-aware memory to future work.
agent_relevance: Failed cases need a tag (do not retrieve as examples) or conversion into warnings. Do not mix them with wins.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Agent Workflow Memory (AWM)
finding: Induce reusable workflows (sub-routines) from successful trajectories and store them as separate items. Abstraction compresses many cases into few.
numbers: WebArena: +12.0 absolute points and 51.1% relative over BrowserGym, 7.6% relative over SteP; +11.8 to +30.7 absolute across 5 websites; about 2.0 fewer steps than BrowserGym and 40.8 fewer than Autoeval. GPT-4 at temperature 0.
limits: Induced workflows can be wrong and lower performance. WebArena tasks come from templates, so in-template gains are easier. Offline Mind2Web action F1 slightly below MindAct.
agent_relevance: Abstracting several cases into one workflow is a compression form of maintenance. Test workflows on held-out tasks.

source: Fang et al. (2025) Memp: agent procedural memory build, retrieve, update
finding: Compared update policies: vanilla append, validation (keep what passes), and reflexion-style adjustment (revise stored memory on failure). Reflexion-style update was best.
numbers: At the final task group the reflexion update beat second best by +0.7 points and cut 14 steps. Memp beat ReAct, ExpeL and AWM on ALFWorld with GPT-4o. Memory built by a stronger model helped a weaker one.
limits: Two benchmarks (ALFWorld, TravelPlanner). Magnitudes read from text and figures.
agent_relevance: Revising a stored case from fresh failure output fits G2 (revise only from real output).

source: Zhao et al. (2024) ExpeL: ADD, EDIT, UPVOTE, DOWNVOTE on insights
finding: Insights are maintained by operators. A new insight starts at importance 2, +1 on upvote or edit, -1 on downvote, removed at 0. Task-similarity retrieval of successes beat reasoning-similarity and random.
numbers: HotpotQA SR: ReAct 28.0, hand-crafted insights 32.0, insights with reflections 29.0, gpt-3.5 insights 32.0, ExpeL 39.0. ALFWorld: ReAct 40.0, reason-similarity 48.5, random 42.5, ExpeL 59.0. HotpotQA to FEVER transfer 70 vs Act 58.
limits: Adding reflections to insight extraction hurt (29.0). Agent with ReAct-only experience (no failure/success pairs) was worse.
agent_relevance: Vote-based pruning of notes is cheap and runs in the loop. Rank retained cases by task similarity.

source: Chhikara et al. (2025) Mem0: ADD / UPDATE / DELETE / NOOP on a fact store
finding: An LLM compares each new fact with similar stored memories and picks ADD, UPDATE, DELETE (contradicted) or NOOP (already present). This is online dedupe plus contradiction removal.
numbers: On LOCOMO it beats other memory systems; 91% lower response latency than full-context; far fewer tokens than full context. The graph variant merges nodes above a similarity threshold.
limits: Conversational facts, not problem-solving cases. The LLM picks the operation, so the decision is not code-checked. LLM-as-judge scoring.
agent_relevance: Template for dedupe on write. For us: do the similarity test in code and ask the model only to merge two texts.

source: Xu et al. (2025) A-MEM: link generation and memory evolution
finding: A new note triggers links to nearest notes and rewrites their context and tags (evolution). Removing both modules hurts multi-hop and open-domain most; links alone give intermediate performance.
numbers: About 1,200 tokens per memory operation, 85 to 93 percent fewer than LoCoMo and MemGPT baselines (16,900). One category score 3.45 vs LoCoMo 2.55 (+35%) and MemGPT 1.18.
limits: Evolution rewrites old notes with no deletion test; drift not measured.
agent_relevance: Local update of neighbours on write is cheap, but needs rollback.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Voyager skill library
finding: A skill is added only after self-verification says the task succeeded; it is indexed by the embedding of its description and retrieved by similarity. No pruning policy is described.
numbers: 63 unique items in 160 iterations, 3.3x more than baselines. Without the skill library progress plateaus later. After 4 failed code rounds the curriculum is queried for a new task.
limits: Skills are code, which can be tested; text cases cannot. Library growth is unbounded in the paper.
agent_relevance: Verify, then add, is the Voyager pattern and matches G3 when the verifier is code.

source: Review of Case-Based Reasoning for LLM Agents (2025)
finding: Theory paper. Lists case-base maintenance as open: dynamic update, noisy or redundant cases. No new maintenance measurements. Cites a code-generation system using dynamic few-shot case retrieval.
numbers: No experiments of its own.
limits: Position paper; claims untested.
agent_relevance: Confirms the gap: little LLM-specific maintenance work builds on Smyth and Keane.

source: Ouyang et al. (2025) ReasoningBank
finding: Distils strategy items from both successes and failures using the agent's own judge, with no ground truth. Consolidation kept deliberately simple (append). Memory-aware test-time scaling adds more contrasted experience.
numbers: WebArena success +8.3, +7.2, +4.6 vs no memory over three backbones. Gemini-2.5-flash 40.5 to 48.8 (ReasoningBank) to 51.8 (MaTTS); Gemini-2.5-pro 46.7 to 53.9 to 56.3; Claude-3.7-sonnet 41.7 to 46.3 to 48.8. MaTTS parallel k=5 gives 55.1 vs vanilla TTS 52.4.
limits: Judge is the same LLM (G5 risk). Authors skip consolidation and pruning on purpose.
agent_relevance: Self-judged retention works on web tasks but correctness is unchecked; our guardrails would add held-out checks.

source: Zhong et al. (2023) MemoryBank: Ebbinghaus forgetting curve for LLM memory
finding: Retention R = e^(-t/S); each recall adds 1 to strength S and resets t. A time-and-use forgetting rule, not an outcome-based one.
numbers: Authors call it exploratory and highly simplified. No quantitative ablation of forgetting versus no forgetting found in the text.
limits: Evaluated mostly by qualitative companion-chat cases.
agent_relevance: Xiong et al. show age-based deletion saves space with small loss; MemoryBank gives no accuracy evidence. Use only as a space control.

source: Smyth and Keane (1995) Remembering to Forget: competence-preserving deletion
finding: Classify cases as pivotal, spanning, support or auxiliary by coverage and reachability; delete auxiliary first, pivotal last. Footprint deletion (FD) and footprint-utility deletion (FUD) keep full competence. Random and utility deletion lose competence.
numbers: Residential property CBR, 50 starting cases, 160 target problems, benchmark competence 100%, swamping limit 75. FD and FUD held 100%. Utility deletion fell to 80%, random to 86%. Case mix: 25 support cases in 7 groups, no spanning; minimum competent base 27 cases.
limits: One toy domain, nearest-neighbour retrieval. Assumes the case distribution matches the target distribution.
agent_relevance: Pivotal cases (unique coverage) must never be pruned even if rarely used; frequency-only rules would delete them.

source: Zhu and Yang (1999) Remembering to Add: competence-preserving case addition
finding: Shows the Smyth and Keane deletion policy can lose competence (no guarantee) and proposes a greedy addition algorithm that picks cases by coverage benefit.
numbers: Greedy addition covers at least 63% of the optimal coverage; the problem is NP-complete by reduction to set cover. Travel domain: 100 states, 10,000 problems, 80 random problems cover 3138; about 15% of cases give about 50% coverage and 50% of cases about 85%.
limits: Single toy domain; same O(n^2) cost as deletion. Requires similarity tied to adaptation cost.
agent_relevance: Greedy coverage selection gives a provable floor; build the library by adding high-coverage cases.

source: Smyth and McKenna (1999) efficient update of a competence model
finding: Competence groups, not single cases, are the units of competence. Footprint cases (largest coverage) represent each group. The model can be updated incrementally when a case is added, using an update set.
numbers: Footprint algorithm adds cases with largest coverage sets until the group is covered. Group competence is the sum of relative coverage of its footprint cases.
limits: Needs similarity-based coverage; text cases have fuzzy coverage.
agent_relevance: A cheap incremental competence map is possible; for LLM cases approximate coverage by embedding neighbourhoods.

source: Smyth and Keane (1995) utility problem framing (after Minton 1990; Francis and Ram 1993)
finding: The utility problem: stored knowledge can cost more to search than it saves (swamping in CBR). Utility deletion handles speed but not competence.
numbers: No numbers beyond the competence results above.
limits: Stated as risk; modern retrieval is fast, so the cost today is retrieval noise.
agent_relevance: In LLM agents the cost is misleading demonstrations (see Xiong et al.), not search time.

source: Leake and Wilson (1998) Categorizing case-base maintenance
finding: Frames maintenance along dimensions (data collection, timing, what is changed). Known only from citation; not opened this session.
numbers: none recorded
limits: Not opened; do not rely on details.
agent_relevance: Vocabulary only, once opened.
